explanation.en: IndexOf('o') finds the first o at index 4. Substring(4, 4) takes four characters from there: "o wo".
Split keeps empty entries by default: "a", "", "b", "" is 4 parts. RemoveEmptyEntries drops the two empty ones, leaving 2.
StartsWith(string) is case-sensitive, so "he" does not match "He". OrdinalIgnoreCase ignores case, and Contains finds "ll".
{0,5} right-aligns in 5 characters. P0 multiplies by 100 and rounds to 26; the invariant culture puts a space before the % sign.

codeSnippet: Console.WriteLine($"{Math.Round(2.5)} {Math.Round(-1.5)} {Math.Round(2.5, MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero)}");

explanation.en: Math.Round defaults to banker's rounding (to even): 2.5 becomes 2 and -1.5 becomes -2. AwayFromZero rounds 2.5 up to 3.
0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary double form, so their sum is 0.30000000000000004. decimal stores base-10 digits exactly, so it is equal.
Count with char.IsDigit counts 1, 2 and 3. char.IsUpper counts B and D, so the result is 3 2.

codeSnippet:
bool ok = int.TryParse("12a", out int n);
Console.WriteLine($"{ok} {n}");

explanation.en: "12a" is not a valid integer, so TryParse returns false and sets the out parameter to 0 rather than a partial value.
Convert.ToInt32 rounds to the nearest even number on a tie: 3.5 gives 4 and 4.5 gives 4. A cast just truncates, so (int)3.9 is 3.
1 << 4 is 16 and >> on a negative int is arithmetic, giving -4. For an int, only the low 5 bits of the shift count are used, so 1 << 33 is 1 << 1.
Unchecked byte arithmetic wraps 255 around to 0. Inside a checked block the same increment throws OverflowException, so X is printed.
i++ yields 5 and makes i 6; ++i then makes i 7 and yields 7. So a is 5 + 7 = 12 and i ends at 7.
& binds tighter than && and ||. false && F() skips F, then the right side F() & F() calls both, because & does not short-circuit.
Sort gives 1,2,3. Reverse(a, 0, 2) reverses only the first two elements, giving 2,1,3.
With no removals, a Dictionary enumerates in insertion order. Assigning d["b"] again updates the value in place without moving the key.

codeSnippet:
var set = new HashSet<int>();
Console.WriteLine($"{set.Add(1)} {set.Add(1)} {set.Add(2)} {set.Count}");

explanation.en: HashSet.Add returns false when the item is already present instead of throwing. Only 1 and 2 are stored, so Count is 2.
A stack built from 1,2,3 has 3 on top: Pop returns 3, then Peek sees 2. A queue is FIFO: Dequeue returns 1, then Peek sees 2.
OrderBy sorts by length first. ThenByDescending only breaks ties, so the two-letter names come out as cy before al.

codeSnippet:
var e = new int[0];
Console.WriteLine($"{e.Any()} {e.All(x => x > 100)} {e.Sum()}");

explanation.en: Any on an empty sequence is false, All is vacuously true because no element fails, and Sum of no ints is 0.
GroupBy yields groups in the order their keys first appear: c, then a, then b. Each group holds every word with that first letter.

codeSnippet:
var parts = new[] { "ab", "cd" };
Console.WriteLine(string.Concat(parts.SelectMany(s => s.Reverse())));

explanation.en: SelectMany reverses each string and flattens the characters: b,a then d,c. string.Concat joins them into one string.
Fib(5) is 5. The naive recursion recomputes subproblems, making 15 calls in total, counting the first one.
S is static, shared by every instance, so three constructions make it 3. I is a separate field per object, so the last one has I = 1.
Field initializers run before the base constructor in C#. So n is already 5 when A's constructor makes the virtual call that dispatches to B.
G does not implement Hi, so the interface default runs and gives I. H supplies its own Hi, which is what the interface call uses.
Generic type inference uses the static type of the argument. o is declared object, so T is Object even though it holds an int.
"ab" + "c" is folded at compile time into the interned literal. Concat at run time builds a new string; Intern returns the pooled one.
new S() calls the parameterless constructor that runs the initializer. default and array elements are zeroed memory and skip it.

codeSnippet:
Console.WriteLine($"{Color.Blue} {(int)Color.Blue} {(Color)1}");

enum Color { Red, Green = 5, Blue }

explanation.en: Members count up from the last explicit value, so Blue is 6. Casting 1 to Color gives a value with no member, and ToString prints 1.
With [Flags], ToString lists the set flags separated by a comma and space. Read | Write is 3, and the Exec bit is not set.
Tuple == compares elements by position and ignores names. a is (1, 2) and b is (2, 1), so they differ; b.X is its second element, 1.
The property pattern checks that o is a string with Length > 3 and binds it to s. s[..3] takes the first three characters.
LINQ is lazy and Take stops pulling once it has two items. Where runs its predicate only for 1 to 6, so it is called 6 times.
Exception filters are tested in order. The message is not "a", so the first catch is skipped; its length is 1, so the second runs.
using declarations dispose at the end of the scope in reverse order of declaration, so b (2) is disposed before a (1).
